name: Tomas Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I load cable and fittings at the yard, then ride out with Martin to repairs and new connections. I like a fault we can actually trace, but I'm still junior and the long checks after a repair can make me feel clumsy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the yard that if AI just sorts the easy forms, that sounds like another office change to me. The poles and wires still need people, and I would rather the new forms list the right parts than look clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am not especially worried about AI in this picture, but I still have to improve at the job. Our mortgage is manageable when my partner's bus shifts and mine both come in, though a lost licence or a bad injury would make five months of savings feel short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the same shifts and ask Martin, our senior worker, to check my splicing before we close the bucket. In the first year I'd put 30 from each pay toward the mortgage principal, so we owe a little less if a lean month comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel reasonably settled, with the ordinary worry that comes from a ladder and a house loan. A small change in forms wouldn't keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Martin still correct?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I stripped too much insulation on a practice joint and he made me start over. It was annoying to start over. The fresh cable cost less than going back after a fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How reliable are the bus shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner has a regular route most weeks and covers the food bills from that pay. When overtime disappears, we can cover the basics, but we put less away for repairs to the house.

say: I would call this a **small office change** while line repairs continue.
I would judge new forms by **correct parts**, not polished wording.
think: I feel my **line job** is likely to continue in this picture.
Our five-month cushion still depends on **two incomes** and avoiding an injury.
do: Keep the same **line shifts** and get splices checked.
Pay an extra **30 per pay** against the mortgage principal.
feel: Reasonably settled, with ordinary **safety and mortgage** worries.
S0.quote: The fresh cable cost less than going back after a fault.
fieldNote: He measures good work by **safe repairs**, and accepts correction from a senior worker without pretending mastery.
Five months of savings and two regular wages make the plateau **manageable**, though injury remains a concern.

steps.text: Keep line shifts and ask Martin to check practice splices
Pay 30 extra toward mortgage principal each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the planners will see the change before our crew does, since software can order parts and fill schedules. I'd want the company to show us a proper job ticket before sending us out, because a wrong isolation point can hurt somebody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office gets smaller, the crews might spend more time sorting bad tickets on site, and I am slow with new screens. I don't think robots will replace us straight away, but I could fall behind other juniors if the work starts being measured by a device I barely know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Martin to walk me through the new job-ticket screen after a shift, and keep a written list of errors to give the supervisor. If my hours are cut, I'd ask the neighbouring utility depot about line openings before I leave this company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary, mostly because the screen may change before anyone explains it properly. Once I have seen it work on a real fault, I can usually get along with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would you record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A ticket last month listed the wrong side of the road for a transformer, and the old dispatcher caught it by phone. I would write down the pole number and date so the supervisor can find the mistake, not just hear me complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow with screens; would you refuse one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, if it's the approved way to get paid work, I'd learn the buttons from Martin. I won't pretend to be an expert after a half-hour demonstration.

say: I would ask for **accurate job tickets** before dispatching a crew.
I would warn that a wrong **isolation point** can cause harm.
think: I may spend longer sorting tickets if **office staff** shrink.
My slow uptake of screens could weaken my **junior position**.
do: Ask Martin for help with the **job-ticket screen** after a shift.
Record **pole numbers and dates** for ticket errors.
Ask a neighbouring depot about openings if **paid hours** fall.
feel: Wary of unexplained screens, but willing to learn from **real faults**.
S1.quote: I won't pretend to be an expert after a half-hour demonstration.
fieldNote: He is cautious with technology but will learn the **approved screen** from a trusted senior worker.
His concern is practical: bad tickets could slow crews, while his **junior hours** may be vulnerable.

steps.text: Practise the approved job-ticket screen with Martin
Record pole numbers and dates for ticket errors
Ask the neighbouring utility depot about openings if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 changes the schedules first, while the robot that can do our climbing comes around 2031. I would ask management to say how many line shifts they expect to keep rather than point to a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 45 at the first date and 48 when robots can do physical line work, with both children still at school. Our five months saved won't carry a mortgage and four people very long if both my line hours and my partner's bus route change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying for the family sports package now and ask the utility for its written staffing forecast. In 2029 I'd keep taking every regular line shift and send applications to the two nearby maintenance yards if our roster starts losing days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel scared, but I know the next sensible thing to do. I can't learn a new trade by the weekend, and I won't tell my partner the mortgage is safe on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the children hear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we are trimming extras, not that they must worry about the house tonight. The older child can still take the school trip already paid for, but we would pause next year's deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the maintenance yards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how to work safely around live equipment, even though I'm still learning line splices. I would ask about paid vacancies and training requirements before leaving a job I actually have.

say: I would explain the **2028 schedule change** and the later 2031 robot date.
I would demand a **written shift forecast** from management.
think: I will be **45 then 48**, with two children still at school.
Our **five-month cushion** cannot replace years of mortgage payments.
do: Cancel the **sports package** and request a staffing forecast.
Apply to nearby **maintenance yards** if roster days disappear.
feel: Scared, yet focused on the **next practical step**.
S2.quote: I can't learn a new trade by the weekend, and I won't tell my partner the mortgage is safe on a guess.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 planning changes** from robots that can perform physical repair around 2031.
His response is deliberately narrow: preserve **paid shifts**, cut one expense and seek real vacancies if hours fall.

steps.text: Cancel the family sports package now
Keep taking regular line shifts through 2029
Apply to two nearby maintenance yards if roster days disappear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my coworkers that five years lets the company show the real equipment and agree rules before anybody's hours change. I'd ask for a timetable in plain words, with the 2031 office change separate from the robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when thinking AI arrives, I'll still have years of mortgage to pay, and at 51 robots can do the climbing. The children will be older, but they won't suddenly stop needing us, and I don't know whether my experience will be enough to keep a post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the training office about a paid substation maintenance course and keep paying the mortgage on time. If a funded place is offered, I'd take it; in 2032 I'd keep line shifts while completing the course and apply for a substation vacancy only after I passed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels less like a trap and more like a timetable I can use. I am still uneasy because I learn slowly and a new course alongside full shifts might be hard at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would make the course possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner could cover a late school pickup one day a week if the class timetable is fixed, but not three surprise evenings. I'd need the utility to pay the class time so we don't lose the mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a substation course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've helped on the outside of a substation and know the safety rules matter more than speed. I would need proper instruction before touching the inside equipment; I'm not calling myself qualified yet.

say: I would ask for a **plain timetable** separating office and robot changes.
I would want to see **real equipment** before staffing rules change.
think: I will be **48 and 51** at the two arrival dates.
I cannot assume older children or my present **line experience** secure the mortgage.
do: Ask about a **paid substation** course with predictable class hours.
Keep **line shifts** through 2032 and take a funded place if offered.
Apply for a **substation vacancy** only after passing.
feel: Less trapped, but uneasy about **slow learning** and family scheduling.
S3.quote: I'm not calling myself qualified yet.
fieldNote: His proposed course depends on **funded class time** and a schedule compatible with school pickup.
He distinguishes limited outside substation exposure from the **qualification** needed for inside equipment.

steps.text: Take a funded substation maintenance course if class hours are predictable
Keep paid line shifts while studying in 2032
Apply for a substation vacancy after passing the course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means the utility can show workers a sequence of changes and let us check each stage. I'd ask for a safety review of the first robot trials, since old line equipment rarely looks like a clean demonstration site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 in 2036 and 56 when robots can do line repairs in 2039, so I will have had time to finish more of the mortgage. The children may have left school, but I won't assume a pension or an empty house pays the remaining bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the line crew for now and pay an extra 30 toward the mortgage each payday while our two wages hold. I'd take a funded substation course if the schedule fits, and in 2037 I'd apply for a paid substation maintenance post after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me a calmer way to think about it, even if the end of climbing work still hurts. I might like the new post, but I need to see its hours and pay before calling it a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to see at the trials?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether a robot can handle the awkward older brackets on the west feeder, and who takes over if it jams halfway up. That answer matters more to me than a video of a perfect new pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what our actual pension statement will say or how much mortgage will be left. If the substation pays properly, I would rather keep working than ask my children to cover us.

say: I would ask for **staged changes** and worker review of robot trials.
I would test machines on **old equipment**, not only clean demonstration poles.
think: I will be **53 and 56** at the two arrival dates.
I cannot count on an unverified **pension** or grown children to pay bills.
do: Stay on the **line crew** and pay 30 extra toward the mortgage.
Take a **funded substation course** if its schedule fits.
Apply for paid **substation work** in 2037 after qualifying.
feel: Calmer with the time, but attached to **climbing work** and cautious about pay.
S4.quote: I would rather keep working than ask my children to cover us.
fieldNote: His longer horizon turns anxiety into **mortgage repayment** and a conditional route to paid substation work.
He wants robot trials to answer a **specific safety question** about awkward brackets and a jammed machine.

steps.text: Keep working on the line crew while hours remain
Pay 30 extra toward mortgage principal each payday
Take funded substation training if class hours fit
Apply for paid substation work in 2037 after qualifying

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast AGI by 2028 picture worries me most because two years is short when the mortgage and school costs arrive every month. A written shift forecast, paid training with a fixed timetable, and clear safety rules for robots would help me make decisions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how the new equipment works on an old bracket after rain. I'd trust a trial more if the crews who know those brackets could say what went wrong and see the answer in writing.

headlineQuote: I'd trust a trial more if the crews who know those brackets could say what went wrong and see the answer in writing.
portrait: Tomas is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with a vocational certificate, a mortgage and two school-age children.
He has about **five months** of expenses saved and relies on both his line pay and his partner’s bus wages.
He avoids unfamiliar tools but will learn an **approved screen** from a trusted senior worker when work requires it.
With longer warning he considers **funded substation training** while keeping paid shifts and reducing mortgage debt.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because his household has little time to prepare for changed hours and robots.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **written shift forecast**, paid training with fixed hours and clear robot safety rules.
